name: Totopara
tagline: Home of the Toto, one of India's smallest communities
meta_description: Totopara guide: who the Toto are, how to visit respectfully with a local guide, the road from Madarihat, the Toto script, costs and what not to do.
summary: Totopara is a village on the Bhutan border, about 21 km north of Madarihat, and the only home of the Toto, one of the smallest indigenous communities in India. Visit by day from Jaldapara with a local guide, as a guest. The road crosses riverbeds that flood in the monsoon.
intro: Totopara sits in a pocket of land between the foothills of Bhutan to the north, the Torsa river to the east and the Titi forest to the south-west, across the Hauri river. It is about 21 km from Madarihat by a narrow road that crosses several riverbeds. The village takes its name from the Toto, a community of Tibeto-Burman language whose entire population lives here. In 1951 they numbered 321; by 2001 the count was 1,184.

Today Totopara is a mixed village. Totos live alongside Nepali and other families who settled here over the last century; the 2011 census counted 2,960 people in Totopara as a whole. The community has a school and high school, a health centre, and growing numbers of young people studying outside. Elders keep the traditional faith centred on two deities, Ishpa and Cheima, while some families have become Christian.

We include Totopara because it is a real part of the Dooars story, and because how people visit matters. This is not a museum or a show. Come as a guest with a local guide, ideally someone from the village, keep the group small, ask before every photograph, and spend money locally. If you want to understand rather than look, Totopara will repay a careful half-day. If you only want photos of 'tribal people', please do not come.

story.title: A language that found its script
paras: The Toto language belongs to the Tibeto-Burman family and was, for most of its history, only spoken. Children learned Bengali and Nepali at school, and linguists worried that Toto might fade within a few generations. In 2015 Dhaniram Toto, a community elder and writer, developed a script for the language, so that Toto could be written in its own letters rather than in Bengali characters.

The script was approved by the Unicode Technical Committee in October 2019 and added to the Unicode Standard, version 14.0, in September 2021. That means Toto text can now be typed on phones and computers. Dhaniram Toto became the first person from the community to receive the Padma Shri, for his work on language and culture. Ask your guide about the script; it is a source of real pride.

did_you_know: The Toto numbered 321 people in 69 houses in 1951 and 1,184 in 2001, almost all in Totopara.
Dhaniram Toto created a script for the Toto language in 2015; it entered the Unicode Standard in 2021.
Totopara is bounded by the Bhutan foothills to the north, the Torsa river to the east and the Titi forest to the south-west.
facts: The Toto community, Bhutan border hills

highlights.title: A guided village visit
highlights.text: Walk the village with a local guide, ideally from the Toto community, who can explain homes, farming, faith and the changes of the last decades. Small groups only, and always as guests.

highlights.title: The Toto script
highlights.text: The Toto language now has its own script, created by Dhaniram Toto in 2015 and part of Unicode since 2021. Ask to see it written; it is one of India's newest scripts.

highlights.title: The road through Titi
highlights.text: The drive from Madarihat crosses riverbeds and runs along the Titi forest, with the Bhutan hills ahead. It is part of a forest-department safari route from Madarihat in some seasons.

highlights.title: Bhutan foothills
highlights.text: Totopara lies about 2 km from the border, with the forested foothills of Bhutan rising directly behind the village fields.

highlights.title: Spend money locally
highlights.text: Buy tea, snacks or crafts where offered, pay your guide fairly, and if a community fund or school collection is suggested by your guide, contribute there rather than giving cash to individuals.

how_to_reach.text: From Madarihat, hire a car or jeep for the 21 km to Totopara, about one to one and a half hours on a narrow road that crosses several riverbeds. A return trip with waiting time costs about ₹1,800–2,800, indicative 2026. Low cars may struggle in the riverbeds.
In some seasons the forest department has run a car-safari route from the Madarihat side through Titi towards Totopara. Ask at the Madarihat counter. Check current status before you travel.
A few shared jeeps run between Madarihat and Totopara for residents, mostly in the morning and afternoon. They are crowded and irregular; a hired car is simpler for visitors.

where_to_stay: Most visitors come on a day trip from Madarihat, where WBTDC's Aranya Tourism Property and private lodges are the nearest comfortable stays. A few families in and around Totopara have offered homestay rooms; if you want to stay, arrange it through a trusted local contact rather than turning up. Facilities are basic. Do not expect hotels or restaurants in the village.
costs: Local guide for a village walk
Tea and snacks in the village
budget_tip: Share the car from Madarihat with another family and combine Totopara with South Khayerbari on the same half-day.
tips: Ask before every photograph, and accept no for an answer.
Do not hand out sweets, pens or money to children; support the school through your guide if you wish.
Do not enter homes or sacred spaces unless invited.
The road crosses riverbeds that flood in the monsoon; do not attempt it in or after heavy rain.
Dress modestly and keep your group small and quiet.

experiences.title: A respectful half-day in Totopara
experiences.summary: Visit Totopara as a guest, with a local guide, in a small group. Walk the village, learn about the Toto community's history, faith and language, have tea, and leave the way you came: quietly, having spent money locally.
body: Arrange a guide through your lodge in Madarihat, and ask for someone from Totopara, ideally from the Toto community. A good guide will walk you through the village, explain the traditional houses, the farming of the slopes, and the community's faith in Ishpa and Cheima, and introduce you to people who are happy to talk. You will also see how much the village has changed, with new houses, schools and mobile phones.

The Toto are a small community sharing their village with many newer settlers, and they have had too many visitors who treated them as a spectacle. Keep groups to four or five, speak quietly, and accept that some people will not want to meet you. Never photograph anyone without asking, and do not push for 'traditional dress' photos.

Ask your guide whether there is a school or community fund to support, and contribute through it. Buy tea and snacks from village shops. Leave by early afternoon so the return drive through the riverbeds is in good light.

faqs.q: Can tourists visit Totopara
faqs.a: Yes. Totopara is an open village, and visitors come on day trips from Madarihat. Go with a local guide, ideally from the community, keep groups small, ask before photographing anyone, and do not enter homes unless invited. Do not treat it as a sightseeing spot.

faqs.q: Who are the Toto people
faqs.a: The Toto are a small indigenous community with a Tibeto-Burman language, living almost entirely in Totopara near the Bhutan border. They numbered 321 in 1951 and 1,184 in 2001. Traditionally they follow a nature-based faith with deities Ishpa and Cheima; some are Christian.

faqs.q: Is it okay to take photos in Totopara
faqs.a: Only with permission, every time. Ask through your guide, accept refusals, and do not photograph children without a parent's consent. Avoid staged photos in traditional dress. Landscapes and the road are fine. Treat people as hosts, not subjects.

experiences.title: Learning about the Toto language and script
experiences.cost: Included with a guided visit; donations optional
experiences.summary: The Toto language, spoken by only a few thousand people at most, gained its own script in 2015, created by Dhaniram Toto. Ask your guide to explain how the script was made and how the community is teaching it.
body: Toto is a Tibeto-Burman language spoken in Totopara. Children grow up also speaking Nepali and Bengali, and for decades there was concern that the language would weaken. Dhaniram Toto, a community elder and writer, developed a script for it in 2015. After years of work with linguists, it was approved by the Unicode Technical Committee in 2019 and included in Unicode 14.0 in 2021.

Your guide can show you what the script looks like, explain how it fits the sounds of the language, and talk about efforts to teach it in the village. Ask respectfully, and do not expect a formal class or a performance; this is part of people's daily work to keep their language alive.
If you want to support it, ask whether there is a community or school initiative you can contribute to, or buy any publications they sell. Do not record people speaking without permission.

faqs.q: Does the Toto language have a script
faqs.a: Yes. Dhaniram Toto created a script for the Toto language in 2015. It was approved by the Unicode Technical Committee in October 2019 and added to the Unicode Standard, version 14.0, in September 2021, so it can be typed on modern devices.

faqs.q: Who is Dhaniram Toto
faqs.a: Dhaniram Toto is a Toto community elder and writer from Totopara who created a script for the Toto language and has worked to preserve Toto language and culture. He became the first person from the community to receive the Padma Shri.

faqs.q: Is the Toto language endangered
faqs.a: It is spoken by a very small community, so it is considered vulnerable, and younger people also use Nepali and Bengali daily. The new script and efforts to teach it are aimed at keeping it strong. Your guide can tell you how it is used today.

experiences.title: The riverbed road through Titi to Totopara
experiences.summary: The road from Madarihat to Totopara runs past the Titi forest and crosses several stony riverbeds, with the Bhutan hills getting closer. The drive itself, slow and bumpy, is part of the experience.
body: Leave Madarihat in the morning in a jeep or high-clearance car. The road runs north through villages and fields, then along the edge of the Titi forest, crossing riverbeds where the track runs straight over stones and shallow water. In winter these are dry or ankle-deep; in the monsoon they flood, and Totopara can be cut off for days.

Look out for birds on the riverbeds, peafowl and junglefowl at forest edges, and sometimes elephants' tracks. The Bhutan foothills rise ahead, and Totopara sits at their foot. In some seasons the forest department has sold this route as a car safari from Madarihat, with a guide.
Use a local driver who knows the crossings. Do not attempt the drive after heavy rain, and do not stop in the forest. Combine it with a respectful village visit and return before mid-afternoon.

faqs.q: How is the road from Madarihat to Totopara
faqs.a: Narrow, with potholes and several riverbed crossings over stones and shallow water. A jeep or high-clearance car is best. In the dry season it takes about one to one and a half hours for 21 km. In the monsoon the riverbeds flood and the road can close.

faqs.q: Can I go to Totopara in the monsoon
faqs.a: It is not advisable. Heavy rain floods the riverbeds the road crosses, and Totopara can be cut off. Go between November and April. In October and May, check with your lodge about conditions on the day.

faqs.q: Is there a safari to Totopara
faqs.a: In some seasons the forest department has run a car-safari route from the Madarihat side through Titi towards Totopara. Ask at the Madarihat counter whether it is running. Otherwise, hire a car with a local driver. Check current status before you travel.

experiences.title: Totopara and South Khayerbari in one morning
experiences.cost: ₹2,500–3,500 for the car plus fees, indicative
experiences.summary: From Madarihat, a long morning can cover a respectful visit to Totopara and a stop at the South Khayerbari rescue centre, with lunch back in Madarihat before an afternoon Jaldapara safari.
body: Leave Madarihat around 7:30 a.m. for Totopara, arriving in time for a two-hour guided village visit while it is cool. Have tea in the village, then drive back through Titi to Madarihat. After a short break, head to South Khayerbari, where rescued leopards and tigers can be seen from viewing areas, for about an hour.

This plan suits families and people who have one full day at Madarihat. It mixes culture and wildlife without long drives, and leaves the afternoon free for a Jaldapara or Chilapata jeep safari. A single car for the morning keeps it simple.

Book your guide for Totopara the day before through your lodge. Confirm South Khayerbari opening days. Carry water, snacks and cash. Do not rush the village visit to fit the schedule; drop Khayerbari if time runs short.

faqs.q: Can I visit Totopara and Jaldapara on the same day
faqs.a: Yes. Visit Totopara in the morning, about a half-day return from Madarihat with time in the village, and take an afternoon Jaldapara or Chilapata safari. Book the safari in advance and leave Totopara by early afternoon.

faqs.q: How much does a car from Madarihat to Totopara cost
faqs.a: About ₹1,800–2,800 for a return trip with waiting time, indicative 2026, or ₹2,500–3,500 if you add South Khayerbari. Prices rise in peak season. Your lodge can arrange a driver who knows the riverbed crossings.

faqs.q: Is Totopara suitable for children
faqs.a: Yes, as a short, respectful visit. Explain beforehand that it is people's home, not a show, and that photos need permission. The road is bumpy, so bring water and snacks. Combining it with South Khayerbari keeps younger children interested.

faqs.q: Where is Totopara
faqs.a: Totopara is in the Madarihat-Birpara block of Alipurduar district, about 21 km north of Madarihat and about 2 km from the Bhutan border. It lies between the Bhutan foothills, the Torsa river and the Titi forest. Siliguri is about 145 km away.

faqs.q: How do I visit Totopara respectfully
faqs.a: Go with a local guide, ideally from the community; keep groups small; ask before every photo; do not enter homes uninvited; do not give money or sweets to children; dress modestly; and spend money locally on tea, snacks or community funds. Treat it as a visit to people's homes.

faqs.q: Do I need a permit for Totopara
faqs.a: Indian visitors do not need a special permit for Totopara as far as we know. It is near the Bhutan border, so carry photo ID, and foreign visitors should carry passports. If you use a forest safari route through Titi, you need that ticket. Check current status before you travel.

faqs.q: How many Toto people are there
faqs.a: Census figures show 321 Totos in 1951, 926 in 1991 and 1,184 in 2001, nearly all in Totopara. More recent estimates are somewhat higher. Totopara's total population, 2,960 in the 2011 census, also includes many non-Toto families.

faqs.q: Can I stay overnight in Totopara
faqs.a: A few homestay rooms have been offered in and around Totopara, but options are limited and change. If you want to stay, arrange it through a trusted local contact in advance. Most visitors make a day trip from Madarihat, which is simpler and kinder on the community.

faqs.q: What is the best time to visit Totopara
faqs.a: November to April, when the riverbeds on the road are dry. Mornings are best for the village visit. Avoid the monsoon, June to September, when floods can cut the road. In October and May, check conditions locally on the day.

faqs.q: What do the Toto people believe
faqs.a: Traditionally the Toto follow a nature-based faith, revering Ishpa, associated with the Bhutan hills, and Cheima, the protector of the village. Some families have become Christian. Ask your guide about rituals and festivals, and do not enter sacred spaces without permission.

faqs.q: Are there shops and food in Totopara
faqs.a: There are small shops and tea stalls but no restaurants for visitors. Have breakfast in Madarihat, carry water and snacks, and buy tea or biscuits in the village. Cash is needed; there is no reliable ATM.

faqs.q: Is Totopara safe
faqs.a: Yes. It is a quiet village. The main risks are the road, which crosses riverbeds that flood after rain, and wildlife along the Titi forest. Travel in daylight with a local driver and avoid the monsoon.
